lessons.title: Feelings, Health & Weather
objectives: Say how you feel, now and in the past
Tell someone what hurts and understand simple health questions
Talk about the weather

parts.title: How Do You Feel?
parts.text: Add the prefix *na-* to a feeling root to say you felt it or became that way: *lipay* (joy) → *Nalipay ako* (Natuwa ako / Masaya ako). For a general state, use the describing word: *Malipayon ako*. It works like Filipino *natuwa*, *nalungkot*.

parts.prompt: "Kapoy na ako." What does *kapoy* mean?

parts.title: Telling What Hurts
parts.text: To say a body part hurts, use *Masakit ang ___ ko*, just like Filipino. You'll also hear *Ginasakit ang ___ ko* (it's aching). For fever: *Ginahilanat ako.*

terms.note: what are you feeling? (a doctor's question)
my head hurts (also said: *Ginasakit ang ulo ko*)

rows: May lagnat ako mula pa kahapon.

parts.prompt: The doctor asks "Ano ang ginabatyag mo?" You have a fever. What do you say?

parts.title: Talking About the Weather
parts.text: Weather words are close to Filipino. Use *Naga-* for weather happening now: *Nagaulan.* (It's raining.)

parts.title: Typhoon season
parts.text: The Visayas gets many typhoons from June to November. Ilonggos often greet each other after a storm with *Okay lang kamo?* and share news about *baha* (floods) and *brownout*.

parts.tip: Look at the start of each verb: *nag-* = done, *naga-* = ongoing or every day, *mag-* = not done yet (planned). The time words tell you *when*.

parts.title: Two Clues for Time
parts.text: The start of the verb shows whether an action is *done*, *ongoing / every day*, or *not done yet*. Time words like *kahapon*, *subong* and *buwas* tell you *when*.

examples.hil: Nagkadto kami sa merkado sang Sabado.
examples.fil: Pumunta kami sa palengke noong Sabado.

parts.text: The start of the verb shows if the action is done, ongoing or every day, or not done yet.

parts.note: Spelling changes when a thing is in focus: kaon → *kaunon*, inom → *imnon*, basa → *basahon* (you will learn these in Lesson 4).

parts.title: Already, Still, Not Yet
parts.text: *na* and *pa* usually come right after the verb or describing word: *Nagkaon na ako*, *Gutom na ako*. For "not yet", start with *wala pa*: *Wala pa ako nagkaon.*

parts.text: *naka-* means you were able to, or it happened (often without planning): *Nakatulog ako sa dyip.* (I fell asleep in the jeepney.) Plain *Nagtulog ako* just means "I slept".

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: Filipino *na* and *pa* work the same in Hiligaynon.
*hindi pa* = *wala pa* (for things that haven't happened).

mistakes.why: for a finished action use *nag-*; *naga-* is for ongoing or everyday actions.
for *kaon*, the done form is *nagkaon* (the Filipino-style *kumain* pattern doesn't carry over).

parts.title: Rest After Lunch
parts.text: In many Ilonggo homes, the family rests for a while after lunch (*panyaga*) before going back to work. People say *Pahuway anay* (rest first).

parts.tip: Watch two kinds of sentences: *Si Nanay ang nagluto* (who did it) and *Ginluto niya* (what was done).

parts.title: The Spotlight Word: ang
parts.text: In these sentence patterns, one person or thing is in the spotlight. A thing takes *ang* and a person's name takes *si*. Pronouns like *ako* and *siya* need no marker. Filipino works the same way: *ang / ng / sa* = Hiligaynon *ang / sang / sa*. Names use *si / ni / kay* in both languages.

terms.note: doer or owner, not in the spotlight

parts.prompt: "Nagluto si Nanay ___ adobo." (Nagluto si Nanay ng adobo.)
parts.explain: in a *nag-* sentence the doer is in the spotlight, so the thing takes *sang*.

parts.text: When the thing is in the spotlight, the verb uses *gin-* (done), *gina-* (ongoing or every day) or *-on* (not yet).
parts.note: *-on* changes some spellings: luto → *lutuon*, kaon → *kaunon*, basa → *basahon*.
parts.title: What Was Done: gin- / gina- / -on
ako or ko?
parts.text: In the patterns of this lesson, use *ako* as the doer with *nag-* verbs (*Nagbasa ako sang libro*) and ko as the doer with *gin-* verbs (*Ginbasa ko ang libro*). Filipino does the same: *Nagbasa ako* / *Binasa ko*.

terms.hil: Ginhatag ko ang libro sa imo.
terms.fil: Ibinigay ko ang libro sa iyo.

parts.prompt: "Ginbasa ___ ang libro." (Binasa ko ang libro.)
parts.explain: in a *gin-* sentence the doer uses *ko*.

parts.title: A Fish or the Fish?
parts.text: A specific thing you both know usually goes in the spotlight with a *gin-* verb. A thing in general usually stays with a *nag-* verb.
parts.tip: This is a strong habit, not a strict rule.

mistakes.why: in a *gin-* sentence the doer is *ko*, not *ako*.
in a *nag-* sentence the thing takes *sang*.

parts.title: Describing a Thing: nga

parts.title: Filipino ⇄ Hiligaynon
bridge: Think in short pieces, not long Filipino sentences.
*Abaw!* and *Amo?* are very Ilonggo; using them makes you sound natural.

mistakes.right: answer, then ask back: *Maayo man. Kag ikaw man?*
use a filler or describe it: *Ang kwan gani…* / *Ang butang nga…*

parts.title: Abaw!
parts.text: *Abaw!* is the sound of an Ilonggo conversation. People say it when they're surprised, amazed or even a little shocked: *Abaw, matahom gid!* (Wow, so beautiful!) or *Abaw, mahal!* (Whoa, expensive!). You've finished Intermediate. *Abaw, maayo gid!*

questions.situation: Your friend says "Indi ako makaupod sa baybay."
You forgot a word in the middle of a sentence.

questions.text: Maayong hapon! Kamusta ang adlaw mo?
questions.meaning: Magandang hapon! Kumusta ang araw mo?
